STM32F411 flight controller

Senior design, wind-disturbance-rejection drone, 2026 to present

Designed, fabricated, and brought up

The flight controller for my senior design drone, which is built to reject wind disturbances. It reads its sensors, logs to microSD, sends telemetry to a ground station, and drives four motor channels, with manual RC control and a remote E-stop.

Microcontroller
STM32F411
Sensors
IMU and magnetometer over SPI; barometer and humidity/temperature over I2C
Logging
microSD
Telemetry
915 MHz LoRa to a ground station
Motor outputs
Four DShot/PWM ESC channels
Safety
RC-receiver manual control and remote E-stop

Design decision

To give us more headroom for faster speeds with the IMU, magnetometer, and LoRa, I put these sensors on separate SPI lines. This made for easier debugging as well, since we didn't have multiple sensors on the same SPI line.

The IMU is the highest priority for the control loop, since it is a part of the sensor fusion for every loop. The magnetometer is very useful for heading, so giving it this clock speed headroom allows for an easier fit into the control loop. Unfortunately, we were unable to use the magnetometer, since the brushless motors were creating fields that interfered with its readings too much.

With all the sensors we had, we only had room for 3 separate SPI lines and 2 I2C lines. I put the barometer and the humidity and temperature sensor on the same I2C line and used the other I2C line for communication with the ESC STM32s.

Bring-up and debugging

For the SBUS signal coming from the RadioLink R8EF receiver, we kept getting a reading of 0 the entire time while debugging, so I went back and looked through my schematics. I noticed that before the inverter IC, I had a 1 kΩ series resistor and a 1 kΩ pull-down resistor. This was unintentionally halving the input voltage, so the inverter was constantly outputting 0 V.

The fix was changing the pull-down resistor to 10 kΩ. After this change, the STM32 was able to receive the signal, and it worked perfectly.

Low Voltage board

Pitt Electric Propulsion, 2026 to present

Designed

The boat's primary low-voltage sensor and control board. It links an NVIDIA Jetson Orin AGX to an STM32, streams timestamped IMU and magnetometer data into a SLAM (simultaneous localization and mapping) pipeline, and relays commands to the thrusters.

Host link
Jetson Orin AGX to STM32 over UART/USB-C
Sensors
IMU and magnetometer over SPI, timestamped
Thrusters
Commands over an isolated CAN bus

Design decision

I decided to have this board powered entirely by the Jetson Orin AGX through its 5 V USB-C port, instead of using the 12 V line we run through the boat. This not only gave me more experience with USB-C but also let me make the board much smaller, since I only needed an LDO for 5 V to 3.3 V instead of a buck converter for 12 V to 3.3 V.

Bring-up and debugging

To validate the hardware quickly, I wrote test firmware for each subsystem using the STM32 core for the Arduino IDE. Its higher-level libraries got each peripheral running fast, and I used Claude to help with code for parts I hadn't worked with before, so I could focus on verifying the board itself.

3-phase brushless ESC

Senior design, wind-disturbance-rejection drone, 2026 to present

Designed, currently debugging

A custom brushless motor controller running AM32 firmware on an STM32, with DShot command input, onboard current sensing, and RPM feedback.

Firmware
AM32 on an STM32
Command input
DShot
Feedback
Onboard current sensing and RPM feedback

Bring-up and debugging

After reviewing the design, I powered up the board and found a missed connection: the gate drivers' OUT pins, the high-side return that references each bootstrap supply, weren't connected to their motor phases. I connected them with enamel wire and got a muffled AM32 startup sequence that faded to nothing after a few power cycles.

To narrow it down, I compared measurements against an untouched channel and lifted the gate resistors for one phase to isolate the FETs from the driver. During this process, I powered the board with both the high- and low-side gate resistors still lifted. The floating gates let both FETs in the half-bridge conduct at once, which damaged the FETs. After replacing them, I held the other channels' MCUs in reset, since without OUT wires their high-side gates were floating too.

I then verified the driver by holding the STM32 in reset and forcing its inputs by hand, confirming the regulator, gate drive, and bootstrap charging phase by phase. I also corrected a BEMF neutral-divider ratio error. Final motor testing is in progress.
